content: The importance of outcomes for individuals or populations directly affected by recommendations is described as their values and preferences. The steering group conducted a review of qualitative data to understand how end-users, such as children, adolescent girls, women of reproductive age, and pregnant women, perceive soil-transmitted helminths, deworming interventions, and their effects. These findings were presented during the guideline development group meeting. In cases where there is uncertainty or significant variability in the values and preferences of the target beneficiaries, a conditional recommendation may be appropriate. A review of qualitative data was also conducted to assess how healthcare workers and service providers perceive soil-transmitted helminths, preventive chemotherapy, and their effects on at-risk groups. This information was presented during the guideline development group meeting. The higher the acceptability of an intervention among stakeholders, the more likely it is to be strongly recommended. If an intervention with low acceptability is recommended, strategies to address concerns about acceptability during implementation were discussed. The evaluation of resource use focused on how resource-intensive and costly the intervention is for service users and health systems in various settings. Recommendations for or against an intervention are more likely when the resource implications are clearly advantageous or disadvantageous. However, a conditional recommendation may be justified if the resource implications are uncertain. An intervention is more likely to be recommended if it reduces health inequities among different groups of women and their families. The steering group presented examples of deworming implementation in at-risk groups across different settings to highlight the feasibility of implementation and identify potential barriers. Greater feasibility increases the likelihood of an intervention being recommended. Each recommendation was supported by a rationale, implementation considerations, and research priorities based on discussions during the meeting. Decision-making procedures were established at the beginning of the guideline development group meeting, including rules for agreement and documentation. Dr. Biggs and Professor Nesheim were nominated as chairpersons, and their nominations were approved by the group. At least two-thirds of the group participated in the initial discussion of evidence and proposed recommendations. Members voted on the direction and strength of each recommendation using a specially designed online form, with abstentions not allowed. If unanimous consensus was not reached, further deliberations and a second round of voting were conducted. If no unanimous agreement was achieved, a two-thirds majority vote was required for approval. Voting results will be retained by WHO for up to five years. The responsible technical officer drafted the guideline with input from the steering group. Technical editing and proofreading were performed by a contracted party. The final draft was peer-reviewed by content experts to provide technical feedback, identify factual errors, ensure consistency with scientific evidence and programmatic feasibility, and clarify language related to implementation and contextual issues. Independent peer reviewers were selected by the steering group, and five of eight approached reviewers agreed to participate. The steering group reviewed all comments and revised the document to ensure clarity and consistency with the original intent. The guideline will be disseminated through the WHO website, including the WHO Nutrition website, the WHO Neglected Tropical Diseases website, and the WHO e-Library of Evidence for Nutrition Actions (eLENA). It will also be shared through a network of international partners, including WHO country and regional offices, ministries of health, collaborating centers, universities, other UN agencies, and NGOs. The WHO steering group will monitor research developments in preventive chemotherapy for at-risk groups, particularly for questions with low or very low-quality evidence. If the guideline requires updating or if concerns about its validity arise, the Department of Control of Neglected Tropical Diseases will coordinate the update following WHO's formal guideline development procedures. As the guideline approaches its 10-year review period, the Department of Control of Neglected Tropical Diseases and the Department of Nutrition for Health and Development at WHO headquarters, along with internal partners, will conduct a search for new evidence.
